claims.statement: TVI-CAMS has no separate backend: a single Next.js app talks directly to one hosted Supabase project (Postgres + Storage) with Clerk as identity, and Supabase holds only internal working copies — TESDA SIS, T2MIS, and BSRS remain the authoritative systems, so nothing in the schema may be presented as official TESDA approval.

The canonical migration 20260528160300_create_tenant_scoped_schema.sql creates the app_private schema, all seven enums, all 14 original public tables, indexes, set_updated_at triggers, every app_private.* RLS helper, RLS enablement on all of them, all public-table policies, idempotent reference-data seeds, and the private compliance-evidence storage bucket with its policies; it is the canonical source for schema and RLS, and new migrations are additive.

The checked-in history defines eight Postgres enums: the seven of the canonical migration — profile_role (admin, coordinator, trainer, viewer), lifecycle_stage (aou, ntp, tip, training, assessment, billing, completed, blocked), batch_status (pending, ongoing, completed, blocked), document_status (missing, pending, submitted, verified), document_audience (admin, coordinator, trainer, viewer, all), assessment_result (competent, not_yet_competent, pending), activity_action (created, updated, uploaded, verified, submitted, deleted, system_note) — plus billing_type (training_cost, tsf_allowance, entrepreneurship) created by migration 8. billing_type mirrors BillingTrackId in modules/billing/domain/tracks.ts exactly, so its mapper needs no enum bridge (contrast DB_TO_UI_STAGE); the assessment fee is absent by design because ADR-001 TVI-scope assigns it to the Assessment Center. The live database and database.types.ts carry only the seven — the file has not been regenerated for migration 8.

Every tenant-owned table carries a tenant_id, and tenant scoping is enforced structurally: composite natural keys are tenant-scoped (batches unique on (tenant_id, batch_code), learners on (tenant_id, batch_id, learner_no), and the three LAMR detail tables include tenant_id in their uniqueness constraints); most FKs use ON DELETE CASCADE, authorship profile references (created_by, updated_by, submitted_by, verified_by, marked_by) use ON DELETE SET NULL so deleting a profile never destroys compliance history, and batches.program_id references scholarship_programs with no delete behavior.

The RLS identity chain is driven by the standard JWT sub claim — no custom claims and no Supabase JWT template are needed (Clerk deprecated JWT templates 1 Apr 2025): app_private.current_clerk_user_id() coalesces auth.jwt() 'sub', then a 'clerk_user_id' claim, then app_metadata.clerk_user_id; current_profile_id() maps that to the profiles row with is_active = true (limit 1); current_role() returns the profile's role. All app_private helpers are stable, security definer, with search_path ''. ADR-006's is_platform_admin() follows the same pattern on a separate axis, reading platform_admins joined to the active current profile.

The tenant/role predicates compose as: can_access_tenant is true iff an active profile has any profile_tenant_memberships row for the target tenant (is_default is never consulted); can_manage_tenant is current_role in (admin, coordinator) AND can_access_tenant; can_read_batch is tenant access AND (role in admin/coordinator/viewer, OR the caller is the batch's trainer_profile_id). can_trainer_write_batch — widened by migration 8 (ADR-001 M2) — is role = trainer AND can_access_tenant AND (batches.trainer_profile_id = current profile OR a batch_trainer_assignments row for that batch and profile); the join supersedes the single pointer, which is retained, still populated, and still read for display.

In the applied base schema, admin and coordinator are indistinguishable — every check pairs them — so the role records who a person is (school proprietor vs day-to-day staff, per CONTEXT.md and ADR-005) rather than what they may do, and both will silently gain any future admin-only capability. The first deliberate split is the admin write policies (20260904120000 — present on live applied by hand, untracked per #230), which scope user administration to current_role() = 'admin' alone instead of can_manage_tenant as a recorded scope decision; migration 8 adds the next split, billing_records' SELECT allowlist, which admits viewer but not trainer. Trainers are batch-scoped (write surface limited to their assigned batches), and viewers are read-only in the app (RULES §1.4 server-denies their writes) with the single applied write policy reaching them being the activity_log append (can_access_tenant, no role predicate) — the one place where the database does not itself enforce the read-only rule.

batches policies: SELECT via can_read_batch(id); INSERT with check can_manage_tenant(tenant_id); UPDATE using+with check can_manage_tenant; DELETE using can_manage_tenant. learners policies: SELECT via can_read_batch(batch_id); a for-all policy gated on can_manage_tenant(tenant_id) covers insert/update/delete.

documents policies implement the audience gate: SELECT is allowed to admin/coordinator via can_manage_tenant, to any viewer with can_access_tenant, and to trainers via can_trainer_write_batch only when audience in ('trainer','all'); INSERT is allowed to admin/coordinator and to trainers who can write the batch with trainer/all audience; UPDATE by a trainer is restricted to their own submission (submitted_by = current_profile_id()) in a writable batch with trainer/all audience; admin/coordinator manage via the for-all can_manage_tenant policy.

Identity and reference-table policies (base schema): tenants SELECT via can_access_tenant(id); profiles SELECT is own row or, for admin/coordinator, rows of profiles sharing any tenant (membership join), with no insert/update/delete policy for authenticated; profile_tenant_memberships SELECT via can_access_tenant(tenant_id); scholarship_programs and program_billing_rules SELECT only active rows for any authenticated user while program_document_requirements SELECT is unconditional; all three reference tables allow for-all writes only to admin/coordinator (plain role check, no tenant argument); activity_log SELECT and INSERT are open to any tenant member (can_access_tenant) with no update/delete policy.

All four LAMR tables resolve access through the parent lamr_reports row: SELECT via exists(lamr_reports r where r.id = row.lamr_report_id and can_read_batch(r.batch_id)); insert/update/delete via a for-all policy granting can_manage_tenant(r.tenant_id) or can_trainer_write_batch(r.batch_id), with the with-check additionally enforcing r.tenant_id equals the row's tenant_id.

Migration 2 (20260705070510) adds trainer_credentials — one row per profile (unique profile_id, ON DELETE CASCADE) holding credential_number, certified_nc_levels text[], specialization, accreditation_expiry — with the set_updated_at trigger, RLS enabled, a SELECT policy for own row or admin/coordinator of a same-tenant profile, and a for-all write policy restricted to the trainer role on their own profile row.

Evidence storage is the private compliance-evidence bucket (50 MiB limit) created idempotently by the canonical migration, whose SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE policies on storage.objects allow operations only when bucket_id = 'compliance-evidence' and can_access_tenant((storage.foldername(name))[1]::uuid) — the first path segment of the object name must be the caller's tenant UUID. The canonical migration created no DELETE policy, so an uploaded file could be overwritten but never deleted (the gap filed during the #41 evidence-storage work); migration 8 (checked in, unapplied) closes it with a DELETE policy scoped tighter than its siblings — can_manage_tenant instead of can_access_tenant, because destroying evidence in a compliance tool is admin/coordinator work only — and that policy is the migration's likeliest failure point because it requires ownership of storage.objects. No ADR-006 policy touches storage, so a platform admin cannot read a single evidence file.

The single shared trigger function public.set_updated_at() (before update, sets updated_at = now()) is attached to 15 tables in the applied schema — the 12 updatable tables of the canonical migration, trainer_credentials (migration 2), and qualifications and tenant_qualifications (migration 7) — while profile_tenant_memberships, activity_log, and platform_admins have no updated_at column. Migration 8 (checked in, unapplied) adds the trigger to six more tables (attendance_records, batch_trainer_assignments, tenant_settings, program_modules, scholarship_cost_schedule, learner_identities) — 21 in the checked-in history — and deliberately not to billing_records, which has no UPDATE policy so a before-update trigger could never fire; its missing updated_at column is part of the append-only signal. execute on set_updated_at is revoked from anon and authenticated, and authenticated instead holds blanket table privileges on the public tables (each migration carrying its own grants), making the policies the only gate.

Migration 3 (20260717054607) is a corrective migration for a hand-created rogue public.tenant table (camelCase columns, int PK, no FKs): it copies the one real record (AKB Technical Vocational Inc.) into the canonical public.tenants by code and drops the rogue table, guarded by to_regclass('public.tenant') is null inside a do $$ block so a database rebuilt from migration history short-circuits instead of failing with 42P01; it was applied to the hosted project on 2026-07-17 and carries that version so it is never re-applied.

Migration 4 (20260831120000) seeds dev operational data: five DEV-prefixed batches (four ongoing, one completed) resolved by tenant/program code and upserted on (tenant_id, batch_code), placeholder learners sized to each batch's learner_count with uli = NULL, and eight document rows per batch joined from the program catalog (the completed DEV-J3ED-002 batch is all verified); it adds the unique index documents_batch_id_document_key_key to close the silent-duplication hazard (failing loudly on pre-existing duplicates, and producing no database.types.ts change because it is an index, not a constraint), while deliberately leaving trainer_profile_id, created_by, updated_by, official_system_reference, and storage_path/external_url NULL so no Clerk identities or official TESDA references are fabricated.

The canonical migration idempotently seeds reference data: tenants AKB/J3ED/NEN, scholarship programs TWSP/CFSP, the 8-key program document catalog (aou, ntp, tip_report, training_schedule, attendance, lamr, assessment, billing_report — with per-key stage and audience, where attendance and lamr are trainer-audience and billing_report is admin-audience), and the 80% 'Billing Preparation' rule per program, explicitly an internal preparation signal rather than TESDA billing approval; supabase/seed.sql is deliberately trivial because this migration carries the real seeds, so a fresh db reset reproduces them.

supabase/seeds/dev_profile_memberships.sql is a seed, not a migration, per ADR-005: it hardcodes Clerk user IDs, and Clerk development and production instances issue different IDs for the same person, so a migration carrying them would run in production and insert rows keyed to users that cannot exist there — dead identities in the table RLS trusts most; it is environment-specific fixture data run manually via psql.

The dev membership seed grants one membership per profile (ADR-005 decision 1): demo@tvicams.app is a viewer scoped to AKB only, and the two human accounts are admins for AKB and NEN; it converges by deleting then reinserting the memberships of its three managed clerk_user_ids because ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE can never remove a stale row and can_access_tenant grants on any membership; is_default is set true for forward compatibility only since it is redundant under single membership; and the isolation assertion it exists to prove is that the demo account sees exactly one batch (DEV-AKB-001) on /dashboard while a scoping regression shows five, verified in the app on the ok snapshot path, not in SQL.

Two type families stay deliberately separate: lib/supabase/database.types.ts holds the raw row types (the Database interface with all 18 tables each carrying Row/Insert/Update/Relationships, the seven enum aliases, and three function signatures — ensure_profile_tenant_membership, current_user_is_platform_admin, create_school) while shared/types.ts holds hand-written UI domain types (Tenant now carrying the six ADR-006 registry fields); only module data/ layers (plus lib/supabase itself) may import database.types.ts, enforced by an import/no-restricted-paths zone covering app/**, shared/**, modules/*/ui/**, and modules/*/domain/**, with the error 'Raw DB row types are data-layer only. Import domain types (shared/types or a module's domain/) instead.'

The regeneration contract (RULES §3.20) requires that after any migration you regenerate database.types.ts and then update affected mappers and domain types; the enum bridge in the mappers (DB_TO_UI_STAGE in modules/batches/data/batches.ts: DB training→UI train, assessment→assess, billing→bill, UI-only entre stage, DB blocked surfacing as UI pending) is a total map, so a new DB enum variant fails compilation until its UI treatment is chosen.

RULES §10 rule 36 ([deny]) forbids executing statements against the live Supabase project without explicit user permission or an agreed plan that covers it — state exactly what will run and why, then wait — and names .claude/settings.json's permissions.deny as the enforcement point: the deny list, by any route (the Supabase MCP server, the CLI, or direct SQL), covers execute_sql (denied as a tool, including read-only selects), apply_migration, deploy_edge_function, all branch operations (create/delete/merge/rebase/reset), the CLI routes supabase db push / supabase db reset / supabase migration up, and psql. .claude/settings.json is a per-machine local registration, not part of the repo: .gitignore ignores .claude/* (re-including only !.claude/hooks/, !.claude/agents/, and !.claude/skills/mermaid/), so the file is not present in this checkout and its deny entries are known from RULES.md's [deny] declaration rather than read from it; the durable in-repo records are RULES.md itself, .mcp.json (the Supabase MCP server registration pointing at hosted project azywaivpyphhsblxjgtn — the single project the rule protects), and the version-controlled hook scripts in .claude/hooks/. Because there is one hosted project and no staging, schema questions must be answered from the checked-in migrations, supabase/seeds/, and lib/supabase/database.types.ts first, with only the read-only introspection tools (list_tables, list_migrations, get_advisors, search_docs) remaining available for what those cannot answer — and list_tables row counts are reltuples planner estimates, not counts.

The Supabase clients implement the anon-key pattern: createSupabaseServerClient and useSupabaseClient build anon-key clients whose accessToken callback returns the Clerk session token (Clerk native third-party auth; the callback is re-invoked on expiry and its presence means supabase.auth.* must never be called on those clients), a missing token throws NO_CLERK_TOKEN_MESSAGE rather than returning null because an anon client would get silent zero-row RLS results indistinguishable from 'no data', and createSupabaseServiceClient (service-role, bypasses RLS entirely) is reserved for trusted server-side writes with no Clerk session.

profiles rows are provisioned by the server-only Clerk webhook path: upsertProfileFromClerkUser inserts new users with the role from a parseable invitation grant (else 'viewer') and only the membership for that grant — least privilege, a self sign-up never gets tenant access — and on update syncs only full_name/email, repairing a missing invitation membership through the ensure_profile_tenant_membership RPC so a failed user.created insert is recoverable on the next delivery, while role and is_active stay admin-managed; deactivateProfileFromClerkUser sets is_active = false instead of deleting, preserving the audit trail while current_profile_id()'s is_active filter cuts access immediately. On the live project the RPC itself does not exist (#230's one real gap), so the repair — and any invitation membership — throws, the webhook answers 500, and Clerk retries into the same hole; a freshly provisioned user resolves to zero rows until an admin assigns a tenant, which the app can now do on live through /users/new (its policies exist applied by hand, untracked) but not through the invitation path.

RLS failure semantics are uniform and silent at the database: no table has a policy for anon, and because every predicate bottoms out in current_profile_id(), a missing or inactive profile row, a profile with no membership, or a membership in another tenant all yield zero rows with no error — the app must distinguish 'not signed in' (the client throws) from 'signed in but empty' (RLS zero rows), and neither unconfigured nor sync-failed states may substitute fabricated data.

supabase/config.toml configures the local Supabase CLI stack for the project (project_id 'tesda-compliance-manager-design-system-v', Postgres major version 17, migrations enabled, db.seed sql_paths pointing at the trivial ./seed.sql, storage enabled with a 50 MiB limit matching the compliance-evidence bucket, and the API exposing public and graphql_public schemas with max_rows 1000).

supabase/migrations/ now holds eight files, while docs/DATA_MODEL.md still tracks only the first seven — no row for 20260910120000, contrary to the ledger's own same-PR rule. Migration 5 (20260904120000) is policy-only (four admin write policies, no tables, columns, or enums), so it never fires the database.types.ts regeneration contract; it is untracked in the live migration table, but #230's verification found its policies present on live, applied by hand — the old ledger's 'pending' status is wrong for it. Its verification seed supabase/seeds/verify_user_admin_setup.sql is checked in, and on live its part 1 (recreating the policies) is redundant for that reason, while part 2's temporary demo promotion remains the checked-in way to exercise the screen.

supabase/seeds/verify_user_admin_setup.sql is a pasteable, two-part setup in one all-or-nothing transaction that makes the user-creation screen observable at runtime: part 1 recreates the migration's four admin-only policies with drop policy if exists guards (re-runnable, the guards doubling as the uninstall, semantics kept identical to the migration) granting admin read on unassigned profiles, role/is_active updates on visible profiles, and membership insert/delete restricted to tenants the admin belongs to; part 2 temporarily promotes demo@tvicams.app (hardcoded Clerk ID — the reason it is a seed, not a migration) to admin on one column of one row, leaves its single AKB membership alone, degrades the tenant-isolation canary until the commented-out revert runs, and is guarded by a do $$ block that raises unless set local app.environment = 'local' (an abort rolls part 1 back too) — though the checked-in file ships that opt-in line uncommented, so the guard is disarmed in the repo copy and the file promotes demo as written. Demo is promoted rather than either real admin account only because its credentials are the ones in .env.local.

The mock-data retirement changed the isolation assertion's caveat: shared/mocks/ was removed entirely and the dashboard renders an honest empty state on unconfigured/sync-failed snapshots (RULES §3.19; selectBatchesForDisplay returns [] for any non-ok snapshot) instead of the legacy viewer-scoped MOCK_BATCHES fallback, so the demo account's exactly-one-batch assertion is only live on the ok path, any non-empty count comes from the live RLS-scoped query, and the DRAFT dev seed's caveat about the mock fallback predates the retirement.

docs/DATA_MODEL.md is the in-repo ER companion and the migration ledger with a same-PR maintenance rule (update the file in the same PR as any migration; move a row to applied only after it has actually run), but its version table — last checked against the live project on 2026-09-06 — tracks only the first seven migrations and has not yet gained the row for 20260910120000; its applied/pending column is superseded by the issue #230 verification, which found the live migration table returns four versions with the school registry recorded under 20260906114735 rather than the file's 20260906130000. Its statement that the live schema is 18 tables and 36 foreign keys remains accurate while migration 8 is unapplied, and its four cluster diagrams still draw the 15 pre-ADR-006 tables. docs/SUPABASE_SCHEMA_GUIDE.md is superseded for implementation (banner dated 2026-09-05) and kept for its design rationale and the TESDA boundary.

Issue #230's repo-vs-database drift is the authoritative current status, superseding the old applied/pending ledger: the live project's migration table returns exactly four versions (20260528160300, 20260705070510, 20260717054607, 20260906114735); the school registry is double-versioned — recorded as 20260906114735 while its file is named 20260906130000, the same migration under two versions; 20260831120000, 20260904120000, and 20260906120000 are untracked; and verification showed the database is ahead of its own records, not behind them — 20260831120000's dev rows are present (batches/learners/documents counts of 5/89/40 match its content exactly, though its documents unique index is of unknown existence) and the other two migrations' objects exist applied by hand. The one real gap is public.ensure_profile_tenant_membership, which does not exist even though modules/auth/data/provisioning.ts calls it. Migration 8 is checked in but unapplied — its own header states it has never been parsed by Postgres — and #230 must be reconciled before assuming a clean db push, although nothing in migration 8 depends on that reconciliation (every table and function it references was verified present).

The #230 drift changes what the old 'pending migrations' narrative implied: migration 5's four admin write policies exist on the live project applied by hand (untracked), so /users/new's direct Postgres path is no longer RLS-denied there and a school admin can be seated through the screen; migration 6's ensure_profile_tenant_membership does not exist (the one real gap), so the membership half of an invitation grant cannot land — the rpc fails, the webhook answers 500, and Clerk retries into the same hole, while the profile row itself still lands because the webhook runs on the service-role client; migration 4's dev rows are present, so the dashboard and the isolation assertion work, but its documents_batch_id_document_key_key unique index is of unknown existence and any new seed using on conflict (batch_id, document_key) may fail without it. None of migration 8's objects (billing tables, billing_type, widened helper, storage DELETE policy, new columns) exist on live while it is unapplied.

Migration 20260906130000 (ADR-006, applied 2026-09-06) adds the school registry: public.qualifications — the national reference table with unique TESDA code, title, nc_level, sector, is_active, and the set_updated_at trigger; public.tenant_qualifications — the per-school registration link row with tenant_id (ON DELETE CASCADE) and qualification_id (no delete behavior), unique (tenant_id, qualification_id), and the per-school facts copr_number (nullable, because a school is routinely entered while its certificate is still being issued), registration_status, delivery_mode, valid_until; public.platform_admins — profile_id as primary key referencing profiles ON DELETE CASCADE, note, created_at; six new tenants columns (tesda_provider_code, province, city_municipality, street_address, provider_type, provider_classification, the latter group unblocking the T2MIS export's hardcoded 'Private'/'TVIs' literals); and an idempotent seed of six qualifications keyed on (code). The COPR/CTPR naming split is deliberate: the column takes the certificate's name while the T2MIS export keeps TESDA's 'CTPR' header.

platform_admins is deny-by-design: RLS is enabled and no policy is ever created, so every operation is denied for anon and authenticated and the role cannot be self-granted through any application path — the deny comes from RLS-with-no-policies, not from withholding privileges (Supabase's default privileges still grant all table privileges on the table to authenticated, verified after applying by a probe in which an authenticated insert fails with a row-level-security violation), and the Supabase linter's rls_enabled_no_policy (INFO) finding on the table is the design rather than a defect; the application learns the answer only through public.current_user_is_platform_admin(), a security definer function that returns only the caller's boolean, never the membership list (modules/tenancy/data/platform.ts caches it per request and treats every failure as not-a-platform-admin, the safe smaller surface); and conferring membership is a statement run against the project directly, gated by RULES §10.

The platform admin's reach is the school registry only: tenants (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE — no DELETE), qualifications (active-row SELECT for any authenticated user, FOR ALL for platform admins), tenant_qualifications (SELECT for tenant members or platform admins, FOR ALL for platform admins — writes platform-admin-only by scope decision P7), profiles (unassigned rows SELECT), and profile_tenant_memberships (all-rows SELECT, INSERT of first members only) — no policy grants batches, learners, documents, lamr_*, activity_log, or storage; granting app_private.is_platform_admin() access to any compliance table, or letting it seat itself into a tenant, is a boundary change that needs its own ADR (RULES §7.30, ADR-006 P3).

The 'Platform admins can seat a tenant's first members' INSERT policy on profile_tenant_memberships carries two load-bearing guards, neither removable: profile_id <> app_private.current_profile_id() — the operator seats other people, never themselves, which closes the escalation (can_access_tenant() resolves purely from membership rows, so an unconstrained INSERT there would let the operator hand themselves everything that function gates in one statement; the first draft, written as a plain with check (is_platform_admin()), lost exactly this boundary and was caught in review before the migration was applied) — and a not-exists subquery admitting only tenants that have no members yet (racy under concurrent inserts, tolerable because guard 1 holds regardless; worst case two seated members); guard 2 is correct only because the companion 'Platform admins can read tenant memberships' SELECT shows the caller every membership row — deleting or narrowing that SELECT silently weakens the INSERT — and there is no matching DELETE policy, because revoking a membership is the school admin's operation.

public.create_school(...) is a security invoker PL/pgSQL function granted to authenticated (revoked from public and anon) that inserts the tenant row and its tenant_qualifications link rows from a jsonb array in one transaction and returns the new tenant id — a school with no registered program cannot legally run a batch, and a partial write would be invisible — while RLS still evaluates every statement inside, so a caller who is not a platform admin gets a policy violation (42501) from the INSERT rather than a privilege; the data layer (modules/tenancy/data/schools.ts) tells the three failures apart: 42501 is denied, 23505 on tenants.code is duplicate-code, and a missing return id is sync-failed.

Migration 20260904120000 adds four admin-only write policies, additively (no existing policy is dropped or replaced, and Postgres OR-combines permissive policies): SELECT on profiles for unassigned profiles — deliberately not scoped to the admin's own tenants, because an unassigned profile has no tenant to scope by, with exposure bounded to name/email of users holding no access anywhere and ending the moment the profile is assigned; UPDATE on profiles for role/is_active on visible profiles, with using and with check both repeating the admin test so a profile cannot be moved out of the admin's visibility in the same statement; INSERT on profile_tenant_memberships scoped to tenants the admin belongs to (can_access_tenant, stopping an admin of school A from granting access to school B); and DELETE on profile_tenant_memberships under the same scope (otherwise the grant is a one-way door and correcting a mis-assignment needs a DBA); user administration is admin-only rather than can_manage_tenant by recorded scope decision, because a coordinator who could grant tenant access while an admin alone could set roles is a split boundary that drifts.

Migration 20260906120000 creates public.ensure_profile_tenant_membership(target_profile_id, target_tenant_id), a security invoker PL/pgSQL function granted to service_role only (revoked from public, anon, authenticated — the webhook has no session, unlike create_school, whose caller is a signed-in operator): it locks the parent profile row FOR UPDATE as a shared serialization point for all calls on that profile, returns without inserting when the profile already holds any membership, and otherwise inserts one with is_default = true — the atomic zero-membership gate makes true correct by construction, and narrows the provisioning invariant so a grant can never add a second school or move someone an admin has already placed; the webhook path (modules/auth/data/provisioning.ts) calls it on both the insert path and the update-repair path, accepts a 23505 duplicate as success, and logs and rethrows other failures so the webhook answers 500 and Clerk retries; tests/unit/auth-provisioning.test.ts pins the RPC call, the duplicate acceptance, and the rethrow.

The /users/new screen's unregistered path parks the admin's chosen grant (role + tenantId) on the Clerk invitation's publicMetadata under namespaced keys tvicamsRole/tvicamsTenantId — Backend-API-only, so the person signing up cannot forge it — and parses it all-or-nothing (modules/auth/domain/invitationMetadata.ts: a half-formed grant yields null and the least-privileged fallback), applying it in the user.created webhook when the invitation is accepted; the registered path runs findUserByEmail (case-insensitive ILIKE with escaped pattern characters plus an exact-match re-check so a wildcard can never assign access to the wrong person, and not-registered ambiguous by design, since distinguishing 'nobody has that address' from 'they belong to another school' would leak other tenants' membership) and assignUserAccess (the role UPDATE runs before the membership INSERT because it is the safer half to stop after, the INSERT always writes is_default: false because an RLS-scoped empty membership list means 'none this admin can see' rather than 'none', and an INSERT failure triggers a best-effort restorePriorRole compensation because a half-applied promotion to admin could read and set roles on the whole unassigned pool).

lib/supabase/database.types.ts now carries all 18 tables — the 15 pre-ADR-006 tables plus platform_admins, qualifications, and tenant_qualifications with the six new tenants columns — and, no longer empty, three function signatures (ensure_profile_tenant_membership, current_user_is_platform_admin, create_school); the ADR-006 shapes were written by hand from migration 20260906130000 and checked field-by-field against generate_typescript_types run on the live project, with two deliberate divergences (create_school's nullable text parameters are typed string | null rather than the generator's plain string, and current_user_is_platform_admin's Args stays Record<string, never>); the file still stubs every table's Relationships as [], the root of the four long-standing TS2352 casts in activity.ts, batches.ts, tenancy.ts, and users.ts, and adopting the generator's real Relationships arrays is a deliberate future cleanup.

Both assignment screens write through the anon-key createSupabaseServerClient so Postgres RLS decides — the service-role client is deliberately not used, its reservation being the Clerk webhook — and they gate on different axes: /users/new on resolveTrustedRole = 'admin' (never the ?role= preview override, which would let anyone preview their way into the Clerk-invitation branch that has no RLS behind it), and /schools/new on the current_user_is_platform_admin RPC snapshot (never profile_role — the two axes are orthogonal). /schools/new works on the live project because the ADR-006 objects exist there (tracked under version 20260906114735 per #230), and /users/new's direct Postgres path is no longer RLS-denied on live because its admin write policies exist applied by hand (untracked per #230); the invitation path's membership write remains blocked by the missing ensure_profile_tenant_membership RPC.

Migration 8 (20260910120000_add_adr001_billing_domain.sql) is ADR-001 Phase 0.1 (issue #36, EPIC #19) and is checked in but unapplied — its own header states it has never been parsed by Postgres, so none of its objects may be asserted on live. It is strictly additive: seven new tables (program_modules, scholarship_cost_schedule, learner_identities, attendance_records, batch_trainer_assignments, billing_records, tenant_settings); columns on three existing tables (batches gains the RQM/NTP authorization block — rqm_code, ntp_number, approved_slots, total_amount, indicative_start_date, ntp_approval_date, ntp_received_date — plus schedule_pattern, total_sessions, five cost-snapshot columns, and entrepreneurship_delivered, all nullable except the boolean so existing batches keep honest nulls; learners gains entrepreneurship_completed; program_billing_rules gains max_absences not null default 4); a partial unique index batches_tenant_rqm_code_key on (tenant_id, rqm_code) where not null enforcing one RQM code = one batch; the partial index learners_uli_idx on uli; RLS enablement and per-table grants for the new tables; the widened can_trainer_write_batch; the storage DELETE policy; and an idempotent scholarship_cost_schedule seed. It alters no existing column and drops nothing.

Migration 8 is single-shot and not re-runnable: add column and create index are guarded with if not exists, but create type, create table, create trigger, and create policy are not — Postgres offers no if not exists for policies, so guarding only some of it would give a false impression that a re-run is safe. It is not: a second run fails at create type public.billing_type. It is safe only when applied inside a transaction, which is how the Supabase CLI and the MCP apply_migration tool both apply it — a failure rolls the whole file back and the re-run starts clean; run any other way (piping to psql without an explicit BEGIN), a partial failure leaves objects behind that must be dropped by hand. The likeliest failure point is the storage.objects DELETE policy, which requires ownership of that table.

Migration 8 deliberately omits three things: no batches.billing_deadline — ADR-003 P5 makes due_date derived and never stored (computed on read from the batch's tranche schedule), the ADR outranks issue #130 per RULES §7, and #130's real defect is the mapper in modules/batches/data/batches.ts substituting end_date, which a column would make permanent; no batches.sessions_held — with attendance_records created, sessions held is a count over that table, and storing it would create a second source of truth for progress free to drift from the attendance it claims to summarise; and no lamr_reports.module_id FK — ADR-001 §11 requires it, but it alters a table holding live rows and changes its uniqueness, so it earns its own migration and its own review rather than being folded into an additive one.

program_modules and scholarship_cost_schedule carry no tenant_id — they describe TESDA programs and TESDA rates, the same for every school, and a tenant_id would not be extra safety but an assertion that two schools can hold different official rates for the same qualification, the drift a compliance tool exists to prevent. Their qualification_code references public.qualifications (the national qualification registry), not public.scholarship_programs (the funding programs TWSP/CFSP) — collapsing the two axes corrupts the billing model. scholarship_cost_schedule holds current rates only: no circular_no or effectivity_date (ADR-001 BB1-prune), because version-safety lives in the batch snapshot — the batch copies its matching rate row at creation. RLS follows the existing scholarship_programs pattern: readable by any authenticated user (program_modules when is_active, the cost schedule unconditionally), writable by admin/coordinator on a plain role check with no tenant argument.

Migration 8's seed inserts scholarship_cost_schedule rows for both TWSP and CFSP × AFFACP211 — 360 training hours, 45 days, training cost 15,390.00, TSF day rate 160.00, and the CFSP-only components New Normal 1,000.00, Insurance 100.80, Entrepreneurship 800.00 (null rather than zero on the TWSP row, since null reads as 'does not apply to this program') — every figure appearing verbatim in ADR-001 sec.3, which cites Circular 015 s.2026; the 'representative stand-in' rates in modules/billing/domain/rates.ts (Rice Machinery Operations, Cookery) are deliberately not seeded, because a missing rate row is a visible gap that stops a billing document from generating while a wrong one generates an official TESDA document with a wrong peso amount. The seed records an unresolved discrepancy verbatim: ADR-001 sec.3 writes Agricultural Crops Production NC II as AFFACP213 while the school-registry migration seeded the same qualification as AFFACP211; the seed uses AFFACP211 because that is the row that exists and the FK requires it, and which code is correct against TESDA's registry has NOT been verified — if it is AFFACP213, both this seed and the registry seed need correcting.

attendance_records (ADR-001 C2/PathA/X2) records attendance per learner per session date — unique (tenant_id, batch_id, learner_id, attendance_date) — with time_in/time_out, a present flag, and marked_by (SET NULL); OCR is deferred, so trainers enter rows manually and upload the signed paper sheet as evidence, and when OCR lands it writes the same rows — the schema does not change, only the writer. Rows stay mutable in place, including after billing, with no lock flag; corrections are expected and each one appends an activity_log event. Attendance-derived progress is the domain fact, not manual typing: progress = sessions_held ÷ total_sessions (B2), where total_sessions = nominal hours ÷ 8 snapshotted onto the batch at creation (E2 — 360 hours → 45 sessions), immune to later circular changes; schedule_pattern stays free text (D3) and affects how fast sessions are consumed and the calendar duration, never the session count.

batch_trainer_assignments (ADR-001 M2) is the (tenant_id, batch_id, trainer_profile_id) join that scopes trainers to batches and supports co-trainers and trainers who work across schools; it supersedes the single batches.trainer_profile_id pointer, which is retained — still populated, still read for display. Migration 8 widens can_trainer_write_batch in strict order: backfill first (every non-null batches.trainer_profile_id copied into the join with is_lead = true, on conflict do nothing), then the function is replaced with pointer-check OR join-check — so at the moment the widened predicate takes effect the assignment set is exactly equal to the pointer set and it grants nobody new access on the apply day, which is what makes the boundary edit shippable without a staging rehearsal, while the OR pointer stays as a second belt so no trainer loses access even if the backfill missed a row; it only becomes meaningful when someone adds a co-trainer row.

billing_records is a generation log, not an accounts-receivable ledger (ADR-001 NoLedger/Y-hybrid): no running envelope, no over-billing guard, no balance — the TESDA Provincial Office reconciles totals and the app must not appear to. Unique (tenant_id, batch_id, billing_type, tranche, version) with a scholar_snapshot jsonb; re-generating after an attendance correction writes a NEW row at the next version, so the history shows the correction (the 'student 5 forgotten' case, 137,000 → 145,200). The append-only property is enforced in the database, not by convention: the grants are select + insert only and the RLS section deliberately creates no UPDATE and no DELETE policy — code cannot mutate a snapshot even if it tries, and adding either policy would silently turn the generation log into a mutable ledger. There is no updated_at column and no trigger, which is part of the signal rather than an oversight.

billing_records SELECT is an explicit role allowlist — can_access_tenant(tenant_id) AND current_role() in ('admin','coordinator','viewer') — deliberately not can_read_batch, which admits the assigned trainer and would let them read the billing amounts for their own batch (RULES §1.5 keeps financial fields away from trainers server-side), and deliberately not can_manage_tenant, which is admin/coordinator only and would lock out viewer (RULES §1.4 makes viewer read-only, not blind); spelling the roles out means a fifth role added later needs a decision here instead of silently inheriting one. INSERT is can_manage_tenant only. attendance_records follows the same two-way trainer/management gate for insert and update (can_trainer_write_batch OR can_manage_tenant, read via can_read_batch), but reserves DELETE to can_manage_tenant: deleting an attendance row destroys billing evidence, so it is admin/coordinator work only — a trainer corrects by updating present, not by deleting.

learner_identities is a thin global identity dimension (uli primary key, full_name) and a future seam only (ADR-001 Q1): created empty and it stays empty in the MVP; ULI uniqueness is by value, not by shared row — the same person at two schools is two tenant-scoped learners rows carrying the same ULI — and the table performs no cross-school double-enrollment detection, TESDA's systems remaining the authoritative lifetime record. RLS is enabled with no policy and no grant — in Postgres that denies everything to authenticated by default (total denial by design): a seam nobody can read cannot leak cross-school learner data by accident, and opening it up is a deliberate act that should come with the decision that justifies it.

tenant_settings is one row per tenant (unique tenant_id) holding the per-school facts for the generated .docx — prepared_by/approved_by with titles, letterhead_ref, addressee, partial_billing_enabled — because ADR-001 W1 keeps the school's own template, plus the tenant-level overrides ADR-001 allows. Its max_absences is a nullable override of program_billing_rules.max_absences: null means 'use the program rule' — a nullable override, never a duplicate default, so the two cannot silently disagree. program_billing_rules.max_absences defaults to 4, not 5: the eligibility rule is absences > max_absences, i.e. a 5th absence disqualifies a scholar for the allowance (ADR-001 Elig; the locked domain fact in RULES says a scholar with ≥5 absences is ineligible).

lib/supabase/database.types.ts has not been regenerated for migration 8: it still carries the 18 tables, seven enum aliases, and three function signatures — no billing_type, none of the seven new tables, and none of the new columns on batches, learners, or program_billing_rules — even though RULES §3 rule 20 makes the regeneration (then updating affected mappers and domain types) part of every migration's workstream. Until it lands, the migration-8 objects exist in checked-in SQL only, not in the TypeScript contract.

The checked-in eight-migration history defines 25 tables, 8 enums, and 52 foreign keys (the 18/36/7 live baseline plus migration 8's seven tables, sixteen new references, and billing_type); the live project remains at 18 tables and 36 foreign keys while 20260910120000 is unapplied, and its unapplied status must not be asserted away — the migration's own header states it has never been parsed by Postgres.
